Solution skeleton:
- Hybrid reduction: a distinguisher between G₀(U_k) = U_k∘G(U_k) and U_{ℓ₀(k)} with gap 1/6 gives a next-bit predictor for some position i₀ ≥ k (the first k bits of G₀ are uniform), predicting f(s_{S_{j+1}}), j = i₀ − k, with success ≥ 1/2 + 1/(6ℓ₀(k)) > 1/2 + 1/(7ℓ(k)).
- Averaging: for fixed s' = s_{[k]∖S_{j+1}}, success p(s') averaged over x = s_{S_{j+1}} equals the overall success; some s'* achieves ≥ p₀. Hard-wire s'*; define φ(x) as the unique seed extending x and s'*.
- Locality: φ(x)_{S_t} is determined by x restricted to S_t ∩ S_{j+1}, of size m_t ≤ γ·m(k); the other m(k) − m_t positions are constants from s'*. Hence f(φ(x)_{S_t}) is a function of ≤ γ·m(k) bits of x: computable by a look-up circuit of size O~(2^{m_t}) ≤ O~(2^{γ·m(k)}) with hard-wired entries.
- Quantify: there are j ≤ ℓ(k) such helpers. Assembled size ≤ ℓ₀(k)² + ℓ(k)·O~(2^{γ·m(k)}) = O~(2^{2δk}·2^{γρk}) = O~(2^{(2δ/ρ + γ)·m(k)}) < 2^{ε·m(k)} = T(m(k)), the strict inequality using ε > 2δ/ρ + γ. Success: ≥ p₀ > 1/2 + 1/(7ℓ(k)) ≥ 1/2 + 1/T(m(k)) since T(m(k)) = 2^{ερk} ≥ 2^{2δk} ≥ 7·2^{δk} = 7ℓ(k). Contradiction with T-inapproximability.
- If instead the windows shared a constant fraction of their positions, say |S_t ∩ S_{j+1}| = γ₀·m(k) for a constant γ₀: each helper f(φ(x)_{S_t}) would depend on γ₀·m(k) free bits of x, so even a single look-up would cost 2^{γ₀·m(k)} — already exceeding the whole budget T(m(k)) = 2^{ε·m(k)} whenever γ₀ > ε, and ε is capped by the hardness actually available (the strong form of the preamble requires ε′ < c, so no arbitrarily large ε exists). With constant overlap the local damage is no longer absorbable: the predictor cannot be turned into a T(m(k))-size approximator of f, and the reduction collapses.

Solution skeleton (the six moves, with hypothesis usage in brackets):
1. G runs in time poly(2^k·ℓ(k)) because f is exponential-time computable and S is poly(2^k)-constructible [(i)]; so it remains to prove indistinguishability. It suffices to show G₀(s) = s∘G(s) fools size-ℓ₀(k)² circuits, ℓ₀ = ℓ + k [a distinguisher for G with size ℓ² yields one for G₀ with size ≤ ℓ² + O(ℓ) ≤ ℓ₀², by ignoring the seed prefix].
2. Assume D of size ℓ₀² with gap ≥ 1/6 exists. The hybrid argument over the ℓ₀ output positions (Yao's unpredictability equivalence, Section 2.5) yields a next-bit predictor C' of size O(ℓ₀²): predicting bit i+1 of G₀(U_k) from the first i bits with success ≥ 1/2 + 1/(6ℓ₀) > 1/2 + 1/(7ℓ). Fix the best i₀ [non-uniformity]; since bits 1..k are the uniform seed, i₀ ≥ k; set j = i₀ − k; the predicted bit is f(s_{S_{j+1}}).
3. Averaging over s_{[k]∖S_{j+1}}: some s'* achieves success ≥ p₀ > 1/2 + 1/(7ℓ); hard-wire it into C' to get C''(x, f(φ(x)_{S₁}), …, f(φ(x)_{S_j})) with Pr_x[C''(…) = f(x)] ≥ p₀, where φ(x) is the unique seed with window S_{j+1} equal to x and the rest s'*.
4. Locality [(ii)]: for each t ≤ j, |S_t ∩ S_{j+1}| ≤ γ·m(k), so f(φ(x)_{S_t}) is a function of ≤ γ·m(k) bits of x; implement each by a look-up circuit of size O~(2^{γ·m(k)}) (entries hard-wired).
5. Assemble C(x) = C''(x, f(φ(x)_{S₁}), …, f(φ(x)_{S_j})). Size ≤ ℓ₀² + ℓ·O~(2^{γm}) = O~(ℓ²·2^{γm}) = O~(2^{(2δ/ρ+γ)m(k)}) < 2^{εm(k)} = T(m(k)) [(iii): ε > 2δ/ρ + γ].
6. Success: Pr[C(U_{m(k)}) = f(U_{m(k)})] ≥ p₀ > 1/2 + 1/(7ℓ(k)) ≥ 1/2 + 1/T(m(k)), since T(m(k)) = 2^{ερk} ≥ 2^{2δk} ≥ 7ℓ(k) [ερ > 2δ follows from (iii)]. A T(m(k))-size circuit agreeing with f on random inputs with probability > 1/2 + 1/T(m(k)) contradicts (iv), the T-inapproximability of f at n = m(k). ∎

Solution skeleton:
(a) Why amplification fails for canonical derandomizers:
- Chapter-2 amplification (Construction 2.7; BMY iteration) composes a generator with itself: the security reductions are required to evaluate the base generator internally (e.g., to place a sample in the right hybrid position). Such reductions are valid only while the generator runs in polynomial time and the distinguishers are (uniform) polynomial time or size-bounded with room to spare.
- In the canonical regime the base object runs in time 2^{Ω(k)} ≥ ℓ(k)²: a reduction from a distinguisher of the amplified generator to hardness of the base step would need circuits bigger than the size bound under which the derandomizer is defined; every amplification step would blow the budget. Also the stretch is already exponential, so iterating/re-seeding (which needs the output to be fed back as a shorter-or-equal seed) is structurally inapplicable: ℓ(k) ≫ k.
- Instead NW achieves stretch in one shot: ℓ(k) output coordinates from one seed via the design, with security coming from average-case hardness of f plus combinatorial control of overlaps — no iteration and no amplification cascade.
(b) Why seed-as-auxiliary-input is possible here but not in Chapter 2:
- Chapter 2: G is polynomial-time; a PPT distinguisher receiving the seed can evaluate G(s) and compare with the suffix — G₀(U_k) would be trivially distinguishable from U_{k+ℓ}. Hence Chapter-2 PRG definitions cannot tolerate revealing the seed, and indeed do not need to.
- Canonical derandomizers: security is only promised against circuits of size ℓ(k)², which is smaller than the exponential running time of G. Given the seed, such a circuit cannot run G (2^{Ω(k)} steps), cannot try all 2^k seeds, and cannot exploit the seed in any way that the analysis does not already account for — and the proof of Theorem 3.5 deliberately establishes the stronger G₀-claim. The moral: 'pseudorandom' is always relative to the distinguisher's resources; when the generator is allowed to be slower than its distinguishers, even revealing the seed cannot help them.
